overview: Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana - National Urban Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NULM) is a centrally sponsored scheme launched by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs to reduce poverty and vulnerability of urban poor households by enabling access to gainful self-employment and skilled wage employment opportunities. It aims to build strong grassroots-level institutions of the poor, provide shelter to the urban homeless, support urban street vendors, and promote financial inclusion and skill development. The mission operates through a three-tier structure at national, state, and city levels, with implementation led by Urban Local Bodies (ULBs).
objectives: Reduce poverty and vulnerability of urban poor households by enabling access to gainful self-employment and skilled wage employment opportunities
Build strong grassroots level institutions of the poor through social mobilisation and institution development
Provide shelter equipped with essential services to the urban homeless in a phased manner
Facilitate access to suitable spaces, institutional credit, social security, and skills for urban street vendors
Ensure availability and access to permanent 24-hour shelters for urban homeless populations
Cater to vulnerable segments of urban homeless such as dependent children, aged, disabled, mentally ill, and recovering patients
Establish rights-based linkages with other programmes for entitlements like food, healthcare, education, social security pensions, PDS, ICDS, financial inclusion, and affordable housing
Promote convergence with schemes of relevant line Ministries/Departments and state governments dealing with skills, livelihoods, entrepreneurship development, health, education, and social assistance
Encourage partnership with private sector for skill training, employment, and operation of shelters for homeless
Support formation and strengthening of Self Help Groups (SHGs) and their federations at area and city levels
eligibility: The primary target of DAY-NULM is the urban poor, including the urban homeless. As an interim measure, the target is the urban population identified as below poverty line by States/UTs. Coverage may be broadened to include families of disadvantaged groups like SCs, STs, women, minorities, disabled, etc., subject to a maximum of 25 percent of the urban poor population. Under DAY-NULM, Self Help Groups (SHGs) of urban poor will be formed, with at least 70% of members being urban poor to qualify for funding support. SHGs may consist of 10 to 20 members, and in hilly/tribal areas or for differently-abled persons, smaller groups with a minimum of 5 members may be formed. Normally, women SHGs will be formed, but male SHGs of handicapped persons are allowed. For the Self-Employment Programme (SEP), the percentage of women beneficiaries shall not be less than 30 percent, SCs and STs must be benefited at least to the extent of their proportion in the urban poor population, and a special provision of 3 percent reservation is made for the differently-abled. At least 15 percent of physical and financial targets under SEP shall be earmarked for minority communities.
benefits: DAY-NULM provides financial and non-financial benefits including: formation and strengthening of Self Help Groups (SHGs) and their federations; access to skill training through Employment through Skills Training and Placement (EST&P); financial assistance for self-employment ventures via the Self-Employment Programme (SEP) with interest subsidy on bank loans; support for urban street vendors through survey, identity cards, city street vending plans, infrastructure improvement, training, financial inclusion, and access to credit; provision of permanent shelters with basic infrastructure for the urban homeless; convergence with entitlements like social security pensions, PDS, ICDS, bank accounts, identity proof, school admission, and healthcare; financial inclusion through opening of bank accounts, financial literacy, and affordable insurance; revolving fund support to SHGs and federations; establishment of City Livelihood Centres (CLCs); training and capacity building for community institutions; and support for innovative and special projects. Under SEP, interest subsidy is provided on bank loans for individual and group enterprises, with no collateral required for loans up to Rs. 10 lakhs, and project costs capped at Rs. 2 lakhs for individual enterprises and Rs. 10 lakhs for group enterprises. Credit guarantee cover is available through CGTMSE. For SHG bank linkage, interest subsidy is provided on timely repayment. Under PMFME convergence, seed capital of Rs. 40,000 per SHG member is provided for working capital and purchase of small tools, with loan tenure of 18-36 months and interest not exceeding 6% per annum.
financial_support: Financial support under DAY-NULM is delivered through multiple components. Under the Self-Employment Programme (SEP), interest subsidy is provided on bank loans for individual and group enterprises, where the difference between 7% per annum and the prevailing rate of interest is reimbursed to banks for timely repayment. No collateral is required for loans up to Rs. 10 lakhs, with project costs capped at Rs. 2 lakhs for individual enterprises and Rs. 10 lakhs for group enterprises. Credit guarantee cover is available through the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE). Under the SHG Bank Linkage sub-component, interest subsidy is provided on loans to Self Help Groups (SHGs) for timely repayment. Under the convergence with PMFME scheme, seed capital assistance of Rs. 40,000 per SHG member is provided for working capital and purchase of small tools, structured as a loan from the Area Level Federation (ALF) or City Level Federation (CLF) to SHG members, with interest not exceeding 6% per annum, of which 3% is retained by the SHG for loan management, and the loan is repayable over 18-36 months. The Revolving Fund Support provides financial assistance to SHGs and their federations for income-generating activities. Funding for City Livelihood Centres (CLCs) is provided for establishment and operation. The scheme also supports training and skill development through EST&P, with cost norms for training providers. Financial inclusion is promoted through opening of bank accounts, financial literacy, and access to affordable insurance. The Innovative & Special Projects (I&SP) component utilizes up to 5% of total central funds for time-bound innovative approaches. The Capacity Building and Training (CB&T) component supports Mission Management Units at national, state, and city levels, with expenditure not exceeding 12% of total allocation. Funds are released through a structured mechanism involving State Nodal Agencies (SNAs), State Urban Livelihoods Missions (SULMs), and Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), with utilization tracked via PFMS and NULM MIS.
application_process: 1. Identify prospective beneficiaries from the urban poor through Community Organisers (COs) and ULB professionals. 2. Community structures like Self Help Groups (SHGs) and Area Level Federations (ALFs) may refer beneficiaries for financial assistance. 3. Beneficiaries may directly approach ULB or its representatives, or banks may identify and send cases to ULB. 4. Submit an application of intent on plain paper with basic details: Name, Age, Contact details, Address, Aadhaar (if any), loan amount required, bank account number (if available), type of enterprise/activity, and category. 5. ULB enters details in a register or MIS and generates a waiting list with a unique registration number for tracking. 6. ULB conducts awareness campaigns through mass media, IEC, local newspapers, and City Livelihood Centres (CLCs). 7. ULB calls beneficiaries in waiting list order to complete documentation including Loan Application Form (LAF), activity details, identity proof, address proof, and bank account details. 8. SULM may develop a standardized LAF in consultation with State Level Bankers Committee (SLBC) convenor bank. 9. Completed applications are sent to the ULB-level Task Force for scrutiny. 10. Task Force calls prospective beneficiaries for an interview before recommending or rejecting the application or requesting additional information. 11. Recommended cases are forwarded by ULB to concerned banks for processing within 15 days. 12. Banks send periodic reports to ULB on application status; if MIS is used, banks may update status online in addition to manual reports. 13. For SEP-G (Group Enterprises), minimum 5 members with at least 70% from urban poor families are required, and no more than one person from the same family should be included in the group. 14. For SEP-I (Individual Enterprises), applicant must be at least 18 years of age. 15. For SHG Bank Linkage, SHGs must have at least 70% urban poor members and follow group norms. 16. For EST&P, candidates undergo skill gap analysis, curriculum design aligned with NSQF, and training of minimum 200 hours for fresh entrants or 16 hours for reskilling. 17. For PMFME convergence seed capital, SHG members engaged in micro food processing with at least one year experience apply via hard copy forms (Form I & II) facilitated by ROs/COs/CRPs, including enterprise details, product category, turnover, bank passbook, FSSAI/GST certificates if available, and photograph of enterprise. 18. Applications are scrutinized by SHG in meetings, forwarded to ULB for approval and digitization in NULM MIS. 19. ULB uploads approved applications to NULM MIS portal after Aadhaar authentication and mobile number validation. 20. SULM recommends applications to State Nodal Agency (SNA) for approval. 21. SNA approves and sanctions amount, which is transferred to SULM’s bank account. 22. SULM transfers funds to concerned federation’s (ALF/CLF) bank account within 10 days. 23. ALF/CLF disburses seed capital to individual SHG members’ bank accounts or to enterprise bank account for group/activity groups. 24. Beneficiaries utilize funds within one month’s interest-free lock-in period for procurement and installation. 25. ULBs collect fund utilization details through ROs/COs/CRPs and enter data via ULB login. 26. EMI repayment is supported by ROs/COs/CRPs, with ALF recovering EMI through SHGs and forwarding monthly reports to ULB. 27. For EST&P, candidates are mobilized, allotted to training centres, and training is conducted with attendance tracking. 28. Post-training, candidates are forwarded to Certifying Agency (CA) for assessment, and placement details are recorded. 29. For City Livelihood Centres (CLCs), ULB prepares Detailed Implementation Plan (DIP) after survey, ensures land ownership, relocation plan if any, infrastructure details, beneficiary list, and safety concerns. 30. DIP is submitted to SLAC for approval, and funds are released in installments contingent on beneficiary list submission. 31. For Shelter for Urban Homeless (SUH), ULB or other agencies operate shelters with minimum staff: one full-time manager and three caregivers (one per 8-hour shift), with at least one woman caregiver for women inmates. 32. For street vendor components, ULB conducts survey, issues identity cards, prepares city street vending plan, improves infrastructure, provides training (1-2 days with stipend not less than minimum wage), promotes financial inclusion, facilitates access to credit, and links to social security schemes. 33. All components require monitoring and evaluation through MIS, monthly progress reports, and quarterly performance tracking.
required_documents: Photograph of enterprise depicting nature and products
Declaration signed by SHG office bearers
Completed application form (Form I & II) for PMFME seed capital
Enterprise bank account details (for group/activity group)
Bank passbook of proprietor (for individual enterprise)
Detailed Project Report (DPR) for capital investment
deadlines: Rolling basis — applications are accepted throughout the year.
implementing_agency: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, Government of India
caveats: Interest subsidy under SEP is provided only in case of timely repayment of loan
SEP-G requires minimum 5 members with at least 70% from urban poor families and no more than one person from the same family in the group
SEP-I requires applicant to be at least 18 years of age
Project cost for SEP-I is capped at Rs. 2 lakhs and for SEP-G at Rs. 10 lakhs
No collateral required for bank loans up to Rs. 10 lakhs under SEP, but assets created are hypothecated
Credit guarantee cover under SEP is available through CGTMSE only if the activity is eligible
Under PMFME convergence, seed capital loan interest must not exceed 6% per annum, with 3% retained by SHG for loan management
Loan tenure for PMFME seed capital is preferably 18-36 months
SHG members must have at least one year of experience in micro food processing to be eligible for PMFME seed capital
FSSAI license and GST registration are encouraged but not mandatory at time of application for PMFME seed capital
Funds under PMFME seed capital are disbursed as a loan from ALF/CLF to SHG members, not as a grant
Repayment of PMFME seed capital loan is required, with EMI schedule to be calculated by ROs/COs/CRPs
For EST&P, training providers must comply with NSQF norms, and course duration for fresh entrants is minimum 200 hours
City Livelihood Centres (CLCs) require Detailed Implementation Plan (DIP) approval by SLAC before fund release
Shelter for Urban Homeless (SUH) requires permanent all-weather shelters with minimum 50 sq ft per person
SUH must provide basic infrastructure: water supply, sanitation, safety, security, and special sections for vulnerable groups
Innovative & Special Projects (I&SP) component uses up to 5% of total central funds and requires bi-partite agreement with implementing agency
Capacity Building and Training (CB&T) component expenditure must not exceed 12% of total DAY-NULM allocation
Funds are released only after submission of Utilization Certificate for at least 75% of funds already released
Interest earned on project funds must be remitted to Consolidated Funds on pro-rata basis
State Governments must transfer Central share received in RBI to SNA’s account within 21 days
State share should be released as early as possible and not later than 40 days of Central share release
Scheme-related funds must not be diverted to other bank accounts except for actual payments under the scheme
Beneficiaries must open Basic Savings Bank Deposit Accounts (BSBDA) for financial inclusion
Financial literacy sessions must be organized for street vendors and SHG members
Training under EST&P must include financial literacy, savings, credit, insurance, and pension components
SHG federation is required to receive seed capital under PMFME convergence
ULB must update NULM MIS with data of existing Micro Food Processing Units (MFPUs)
City Nodal Officer for PMFME should preferably be the Municipal Commissioner
State Nodal Officer for PMFME should preferably be the State Mission Director
ROs/COs/CRPs must support SHGs in preparing applications, enterprise upgradation plans, and EMI schedules
Applications for PMFME seed capital are processed in online mode only via NULM MIS portal
Online application requires Aadhaar authentication and mobile number validation
Once applied for seed capital, beneficiaries cannot submit another application from MIS database
SULM may reject applications citing reasons, and rejected applications may be reconsidered at ULB level
SNA may reject applications, and SULM may forward them to ULB for re-consideration
Fund release details must be entered in PFMS module of NULM MIS by SNA and SULM
Utilization data must be collected by ULB through ROs/COs/CRPs and entered via ULB login
Dashboard for PMFME implementation is incorporated in the IT module of NULM MIS
